books.section: American Involvement in Vietnam, World War II–1963

primary_sources: John Kerry, testimony to the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, April 22, 1971 (paraphrased)

source: original; stimulus paraphrased from the grounding books' account of Vietnam Veterans Against the War

stimulus.source_note: Paraphrase of the veterans' antiwar movement, from the grounding books.
stimulus.text: Paraphrase of the veterans' antiwar movement. Vietnam Veterans Against the War was formed in 1967. In early 1971, more than 150 veterans testified in Detroit at the Winter Soldier Investigation, describing war crimes they said they had seen or taken part in. In April 1971 the veterans marched in Washington, and John Kerry carried their testimony to the Senate Foreign Relations Committee.

stem: Why did testimony from veterans like Kerry carry special weight in the debate over the war?

options.text: Veterans were the only Americans allowed to speak about the war in public
options.misconception: Background: many Americans spoke about the war in public, including students, clergy, and politicians.

options.text: Veterans had supported the war without question until 1971 arrived
options.misconception: Veterans had questioned the war for years; the group itself was formed in 1967.

options.text: The Senate had ordered all veterans to testify against the war
options.misconception: Background: the Senate heard Kerry's testimony; it never ordered veterans to testify against the war.

options.text: Veterans spoke from firsthand service, so criticism could not be dismissed as ignorance

rationales.A: Background: students, clergy, politicians, and many others spoke publicly about the war, so veterans were not the only voices.
rationales.B: Background: the veterans' group was formed in 1967, so veterans had questioned the war for years before 1971.
rationales.C: Background: the Senate heard Kerry's testimony at a hearing; it never ordered veterans to testify against the war.
rationales.D: Background: these veterans had served in Vietnam, so their criticism came from firsthand experience of the fighting.
rationales.general:
1. The passage shows veterans organizing their own antiwar group as early as 1967.
2. Background: in 1971 more than 150 of them testified in Detroit about what they had seen or done.
3. Background: their spokesman then carried that testimony to the Senate, wearing his uniform and medals.
4. A critic who has fought the war is hard to dismiss as someone who does not understand it, and that is why their words carried weight.
Remember: A witness who was there is harder to dismiss than a witness who was not.
